To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) exporters’ productivity gains are mediated by innovativeness, human capital, and production capability; (2) the effect of exporting on innovativeness is more salient for non-state-owned enterprises than for state-owned enterprises; (3) the effect of innovativeness on production capability is more salient when export intensity is medium or high than when it is low or when new product development intensity is medium or low than when it is high; (4) the effect of production capability

exporters utilize strategic decision-making in the areas of innovativeness, human capital, and production capability to leverage knowledge and resource gained from exporting, and that the effectiveness of these mechanisms is contingent upon industry and ownership characteristics.

the learning-by-export (LBE) model, which is based on the assumption that exporters utilize strategic decision variables to leverage knowledge obtained from exporting, is a better model than a conventional LBE model that does not include the strategic variables.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: how does exporting lead to firm-level productivity gains, and under what conditions does exporting have this effect?
how and under what circumstances do firms achieve productivity gain by exporting, conventionually known as the learning by exporting (LBE) hypothesis.
how and under what circumstances do firms achieve productivity gain from exporting, a topic of considerable importance for both academic research and business practice.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the multimediation model of LBE is valid and that the salience is conditional on the ownership structure and industry context.
the multimediation mechanism of learning by exporting model provides a better understanding of the learning-by-export phenomenon and its implications for firms and the economy.

our results suggest that firms that are non-state-owned and operate in industries with medium or high new product development intensities are more likely to achieve productivity gains through the strategic decisions pertinent to production capability, innovativeness, and human capital, which in turn are contingent upon the knowledge and resources obtained through export activities.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the LBE effect is a multimediation process.
firms can leverage the LBE effect by utilizing their resources and knowledge in the right way, and that the effectiveness of these mechanisms varies with ownership structure and industry context.
firms should leverage their knowledge and resources obtained through exporting in order to enhance production capability, human capital, and innovativeness, so as to achieve productivity gains.
The main takeaway from our work is that
exporting is not only a means to an end but also an end in itself.
the learning-by-export hypothesis can be further refined by considering the role of strategic decisions and the contingent nature of these decisions.
the LBE effect is not a one-dimensional, linear, causal process.
